K4 to be checked from 3.1.1.14 (21b2).
When he is about to depart on a journey, he first gives instructions regarding whatever needs to be instructed.

3.1.1.2. Having placed the sacred thread over his left shoulder and sipped water, standing in the sacrificer’s place, he pays homage to the Āhavanīya fire with the verse: “O Agni Jātavedas, may I bear my first name.”
3.1.1.3. Or else, he goes forth while restraining his speech. 3.1.1.4. When he indeed restrains his speech, then speech ascends into the mind.
3.1.1.5. Now, that which is the mind is breath; and that which is breath is the uninjured deity. Having caused speech to ascend into that uninjured deity, he departs on his journey.
3.1.1.6. Having concealed himself either with a house or a tree, he releases his speech.

3.1.1.7. The observance for him while away on a journey is as follows: he does not speak untruth; he does not eat meat; he does not approach a woman; they do not wash his garment by means of a washing-basin; he sleeps on the ground; he sleeps in the eastern shade; he eats his meal before [the sun has risen], or he observes a milk-vow; he fetches the fuel-wood before sunrise; he kindles the fire; and he does not remain away from home for more than twelve days. 3.1.1.8.
Just as he puts on the divine garments, so he returns to his home after having been away on a journey.
3.1.1.9. He prepares a fuel-stick from a path.
3.1.1.10. Having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech.
3.1.1.11. When he indeed restrains his speech, then speech ascends into the mind.

3.1.1.12. Now, that which is the mind is indeed the breath; and that which is the breath is the unafflicted deity. Having thus ascended into the unafflicted deity, he returns again. 3.1.1.13. Having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and sipped water, standing in the sacrificer’s station, he exchanges places with the Āhavanīya fire, saying: "O Jātavedas, my name and yours are one; you are the most excellent Gandharva. 3.1.1.14. He silently places a third fuel-stick upon the fire.
3.1.1.15. Having approached the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he silently places a third fuel-stick upon it.

3.1.1.16. Having stepped forward toward the *gārhapatya* fire, he worships it with: "O Agni, through thee may my fathers [attain] well-being; place me in happiness. 3.1.1.17. He silently places a third fuel-stick upon it.
3.1.1.18 Then, having gone forward to the east, he piles grass around the Āhavanīya fire.
3.1.1.19 He fans the embers with the verse: “May this Agni be most excellent; may there be great heroic power for him.

3.1.1.20 Then, sitting on grass or a bundle of grass in the sacrificer’s place, he addresses those who are to be addressed and converses with those with whom he ought to converse. This is the ritual attendance upon the divine.

3.1.1.21. Thus indeed did the gods worship; thus did the seers; thus did those former ones who were learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and seekers of truth (*ṛtāyu*). But nowadays, this has fallen into disuse due to the weightiness of the vow and because of knowledge; there is no Brāhmaṇa-explanation for the recitation of the Vāta[-hymn], nor for the *nṛmṇa* meter; this is simply a Brāhmaṇa-text. 3.1.1.22. Regarding this, it is said: "One should desire to attain it even in a single night; one should desire to attain the divine. This now is the worship of the divine. 3.1.1.23. Now, therefore, follow the steps of the Virāj.
3.1.1.24. "He is about to worship with the *virāj* verses; he instructs him beforehand"—this is the same [as before].

3.1.1.25. Having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, standing behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he worships it [with the formula]: "O manly one, protect my offspring."

3.1.1.26. With the words, “O Atharvan, protect my food,” he addresses the Anvāhāryapacana fire; with “O Śaṃsya, protect my cattle,” the Āhavanīya fire; with “O Sapratha, protect my assembly hall,” the Sabhya fire; with “O Ahe Budhniya, protect my mantra,” the Āvasathīya fire; and with “Homage be to you! Protect me,” he addresses all of them together.
3.1.1.27. Then, restraining his speech, he goes forth. 3.1.1.28. “Whenever one restrains his speech”—this is the same [as before].

3.1.1.29. Having concealed himself with a house or a tree, he releases his speech. 3.1.1.30. For him who is traveling, the rule is: sleeping at will, reclining at will, and adorning oneself at will; for one who travels, there is no limit as long as he desires. Having traveled as far as he wishes, he returns home. 3.1.1.31. From the road, he prepares a fuel-stick.
3.1.1.32. Having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech.
3.1.1.33. "Whenever he restrains his speech"—this is the same [as before].

3.1.1.34. Having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire, he worships it with: "O noble one, you have protected my offspring; protect that for me."
3.1.1.35. He silently places a third fuel-stick on the Anvāhāryapacana fire with the mantra: “O Atharvan, you have protected my father; protect him for me. 3.1.1.36.
He silently places a third fuel-stick on it or sets it down near it.
3.1.1.37. [He addresses] the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: “O Śaṃsyā, you have protected my cattle; protect them for me.”
3.1.1.38. They silently place a third fuel-stick upon the fire, or they set it down near it.
3.1.1.39. "O wide-spreading one, you have protected my assembly hall; protect that for me," [with these words] he addresses the *sabhya* fire.
3.1.1.40. "O abyss-dwelling one, you have protected my secret counsel; protect that for me," [with these words] he addresses the *āvasathīya* fire.
3.1.1.41. "Homage be to you! You have protected me; protect me!"—with these words, he should worship all of them together.

3.1.1.42. Then, "having sat down on grass or a bundle of grass in the sacrificer’s seat"—the rest is the same as before. 3.1.1.43. If he were to worship with the words "you have protected, you have protected," they would consider him to have a protector while he is away on a journey, not when he is living together [with his family].

3.1.1.44. When he approaches with the words, "You have protected [them]; protect [them]," it is just as his guardians think of him while he is away on a journey, so they think of him while he dwells together with them. Therefore, he should approach with the words, "You have protected them; protect them for me. Thus ends the Virājakrama section. 3.1.1.X. Now, therefore, follows the Māhācamasa. 3.1.2. [N1,28a5; 1081B 100]

3.1.2.1. Now, therefore, [concerning] the Mahācamasa cup. 3.1.2.2. When he is about to worship with the Mahācamasa, he first gives instructions—this is the same [as before]. 3.1.2.3. Having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and sipped water, standing behind the Gārhapatya fire, he worships it, saying: "Fearlessness for thee; grant me fearlessness; protect me from the fear of men."

3.1.2.4. With the words, “Fearlessness for you, fearlessness for me,” he addresses the Anvāhāryapacana fire; with the words, “Protect me from the fear of the ancestors. 3.1.2.5. With the words, “Fearlessness for you, fearlessness for me,” he addresses the Āhavanīya fire; with the words, “Protect me from the fear of the gods.
3.1.2.6. With the words, “Homage be to you; protect me,” he addresses all of them together.

3.1.2.7. Or else, he goes forth while restraining his speech. 3.1.2.8. "For when one indeed releases his speech"—this is the same [as before]. 3.1.2.9. Having concealed himself with a house or a tree, he releases his speech.
3.1.2.10. The vow for him while he is away on a journey:
3.1.2.11. Just as in the case of the Virāj-kramas, so does he return to his home after having been away. 3.1.2.12. From the road, he prepares a fuel-stick.
3.1.2.13. Having looked back at the fires, he restrains his speech. 3.1.2.14.
"Whenever one restrains one's speech"—this is the same [as before].

3.1.2.15. Having placed the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder and having sipped water, standing in the sacrificer’s place, he worships the Āhavanīya fire with: "Fearlessness for thee; fearlessness for me. Protect me from divine fear; therefore, protect me from fear."
3.1.2.16. He silently places a third fuel-stick on the fire, or he sets it down near it.

3.1.2.17. With the formula, "Fearlessness for thee, fearlessness for me," he addresses the Anvāhāryapacana fire: "Thou hast protected me from the fear of the ancestors; therefore, protect me from fear. 3.1.2.18. He silently places a third fuel-stick on the fire, or he sets it down near it.
3.1.2.19. With the words, "Fearlessness for you, fearlessness for me," he offers a fuel-stick to the Gārhapatya fire.
3.1.2.20. With the words, "You have protected me from human fear; therefore, protect me from that fear," 3.1.2.21.
he silently places a third fuel-stick on the fire or sets it down near it.
3.1.2.22. "Homage be to you; protect me, guard me"—with these words [he addresses] all [the priests] together.
3.1.2.23. Then, "having sat down upon grass or a bundle of grass in the sacrificer's seat"—this is the same as before.

3.1.2.24. "This world, indeed, is the *gārhapatya* fire; the intermediate space is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire; and the heavenly world is the *āhavanīya* fire. When he is about to go on a journey and worships [the fires] from here toward the distance, he departs after having caused these worlds to ascend [within himself]. For him who is traveling abroad, there shall never be any affliction or injury. If, upon returning, he were to worship them in this same manner, he would fall away from these worlds and would quickly depart from this world. Therefore, he [should worship] again..."
"Come from there to here; approach us!"—thus he establishes himself in these very worlds; he does not meet with misfortune, and he reaches a full lifespan.
Day after day, indeed, these [sacrificial fires] fear evil, thinking: "He will find no faith; he will snatch away our faith and wealth, or he will first cast us down into the fire. 3.1.2.25.

3.1.2.26. With the words, “That which is fearlessness for you, may that be fearlessness for me,” he worships [the fire]. He thus bestows fearlessness upon these [ancestors]. When fearlessness has been granted to them, they grant fearlessness to him. Indeed, there are three kinds of fears: those pertaining to the gods, those pertaining to the ancestors, and those pertaining to humans.

3.1.2.27. “This indeed is the divine [rite] for one who fears the lack of a world; this is the ancestral [rite] for one who fears the lack of offspring; and this is the human [rite] for one who fears the lack of cattle. No fear comes to him from the gods, nor from the ancestors, nor from men, who worships with this,” so said Māhācamasa. 3.1.2.28. Now, therefore, follows the expiation for a broken [sacrifice].

3.1.2.29. If they should report to him any mishap during the sacrifice (*yajñārti*)—such as: "The sun has set," or "It has risen," or "They have drawn water," or "The water-jar has been lifted up or set down," or "A cart or a chariot has passed between [the fires]," or "The *agnihotrī* cow has sat down," or "While the *agnihotra* oblation was being placed on the fire, a dog passed between [the fires]"; or if they should report any other such mishap during the sacrifice; 3.1.2.30.

Having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, having purified it, having cleansed both the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles, and having gone forward toward the east, he takes four portions of butter at the *āhavanīya* fire.

3.1.2.31. He offers that [oblation] with: "May the mind enjoy the clarified butter as its light; may it join together this interrupted sacrifice. Those dawns and those sunsets which have passed—those I unite by means of the oblation of ghee, svāhā!

3.1.2.32. Just as one would join oneself to oneself, or join a joint with a ligament, or glue a piece of leather or something else [to a surface], even so does he join what was torn in the sacrifice and restore it. 3.1.2.33. Indeed, no affliction whatsoever occurs, nor any injury, where this expiation is performed.

3.1.2.34. Now, in former times, when those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) had stayed for ten nights anywhere at all, they considered that [period] to be a state of interrupted ritual form. They used to offer this [oblation]. Regarding this, they say: "One should not offer when the narrative is different; it would be as if a dancer were to perform a distorted dance, or as if one were to treat a patient who is not ill. Therefore, one should not offer when the narrative is different. Thus, he offers when the narrative is different. 3.1.2.35. "This is the established rule"—thus there is an uninterrupted expiation (*prāyaścitti*). 3.1.2.36. Now, therefore, concerning the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel).

3.1.3 [K3,36a3; N1,29a7; T1,102; C34] 3.1.3.1. Now, therefore, concerning the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel). 3.1.3.2. Regarding this, some indeed perform the *anvādhāna* of the fires immediately after having offered the *agnihotra* at the end of the night, saying: "From the *agnihotra*, sacrifices are extended; thus we shall connect the sacrifice with the *agnihotra*."

3.1.3.3. Now there is indeed a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Just as those for whom the Soma has been pressed together, so too are these for whom the sacrifice has been prepared together; they shall sacrifice on the morrow. Thus, the former [sacrificers] spoke, saying, "We shall take possession of the deities. 3.1.3.4. If one were to act in this manner, it would be as if one were to offer hospitality to one who has not yet arrived. 3.1.3.5. It would be just as if one were to wish to seize one who has not yet arrived; such is that.
3.1.3.6. Now, some add the fuel after the sun has risen, saying, "In this way we shall win over the deities. 3.1.3.7.

If one were to do so, it would be as if he were to offer hospitality to a guest who has already departed. 3.1.3.8. It would be just as if he were to seek to win back what has already been lost. Such is that act.
3.1.3.9. One should add the fuel when the sun is devoid of rays. For the fire here heats by its flame and smoke, while yonder sun heats by its brilliance and rays; these two meet here. 3.1.3.10.

Just as one would embrace them when they have met, or gratify them when they have met—such is that act of adding fuel when the sun is devoid of rays. Thus he adds the fuel when the sun is indeed devoid of rays; this is the established rule.
3.1.3.11. Of the *vihavya* verses, he offers one with the first verse at the Āhavanīya fire, two silently; three silently at the Gārhapatya fire, and three silently at the Anvāhāryapacana fire.
3.1.3.12. Having gone forward, he places the fourth fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire before the rite is concluded.

3.1.3.13. Then, standing in the sacrificer’s place, he worships with the seven following verses. Now, having added fuel in this same manner for one [fire], he does not worship; then for another, he uses the first of the *vihavyā* verses for the Āhavanīya fire, and two silently. With the verse "O Agni, those born," he addresses the Gārhapatya fire, and two silently. With the verse "Those born by force," he addresses the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and two silently. Having gone forward, he places the fourth log on the Āhavanīya fire before the rite is concluded, [with the verse] "Indra hitherward..."
"From there we invoke him who wins cattle, wins wealth, and wins horses; who, at our invocation, may enjoy this sacrifice of ours—O possessor of bay horses, protect this rite for us; svāhā!
(3.1.3.14). Then, standing on the sacrificer’s station, he worships with the next seven verses (3.1.3.15). Now, having added fuel in this same manner once, he does not worship.
3.1.3.16. Now, they call this "the near [fire]". 3.1.3.17.
Then, from the *vihavya* verses themselves, one verse is offered with the first [verse] into the Āhavanīya fire, and two silently.
3.1.3.18. With the second [verse], one verse is offered into the Gārhapatya fire, and two silently.

3.1.3.19. With the third [verse], he places one log on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and two silently. 3.1.3.20. Having gone forward, he places the fourth log on the Āhavanīya fire before the conclusion of the rite.
3.1.3.21. Then, standing in the sacrificer’s place, he worships twice with the following verses.
3.1.3.22. Now, having added fuel in this very manner for one [fire], he does not perform the *upatiṣṭhana* (reverential standing).

3.1.3.23. Now, for one [fire], he offers with three verses; for the *āhavanīya*, with three [verses] each; for the *gārhapatya*, with three [verses] each; for the *anvāhāryapacana*, with two [verses]; and for one [fire], silently. 3.1.3.24.
Having gone forward, he places the fourth [piece of fuel] on the *āhavanīya* before the conclusion [of the rite].

3.1.3.25. Then, standing at the sacrificer’s station, he worships with the two following [verses]. 3.1.3.26. Now, having added fuel in this very same manner for one [fire], he does not perform the worship.
3.1.3.27. Now, for another [fire], he offers three [verses] to the Āhavanīya, three to the Gārhapatya, three to the Anvāhāryapacana with two [verses], and one silently.

3.1.3.28. Having gone forward, he places the fourth kindling-stick on the Āhavanīya fire before the completion [of the rite]. 3.1.3.29. Then, standing on the sacrificer’s seat, he pays reverence with the two following [verses]. 3.1.3.30. Now, having added fuel in this very same manner once more, he does not pay reverence.
3.1.3.31. "Then, with one [verse] each, he places [fuel] on the Āhavanīya fire; with three [verses] each, on the Gārhapatya fire; ... one silently. 3.1.3.32.

Having gone forward to the east, he places the fourth [piece of fuel] on the Āhavanīya fire before the conclusion [of the rite]. 3.1.3.33. He does not perform the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) here.

3.1.3.34. Now, as for the manner of piling [the fires]: with the formula "Bhūḥ," he makes three offerings on the Gārhapatya; with "Bhuvaḥ," three on the Anvāhāryapacana; and with "Suvaḥ," three on the Āhavanīya. 3.1.3.35.
This indeed they call "the manner of piling according to the established order. 3.1.3.36.
"Whichever among these he may desire, that he should perform"—this is the rule regarding the adding of fuel (anvādhāna); now, therefore, follows the entering upon the vow (vrata-upāyana).
3.1.3.37. Now, some indeed enter upon the vow after having merely added fuel to the fires.

3.1.3.38. [They do this] thinking, "Thus, when we have entered upon the vow, they will perform whatever task is to be done with a *yajus* formula—thinking, 'Having fetched the branch with a *yajus* formula, they will drive away the calves with a *yajus* formula.
3.1.3.39. Then, standing to the south, he enters upon the vow.
3.1.3.40. “For Indra, having stepped forth again and again, slew Vṛtra through prosperity,” so says the Brāhmaṇa. 3.1.3.41.
With the words, “The plants are rich in milk,” he sips water across the filter with the formula, “Rich in milk, mingle with the plants.

3.1.3.42. Having performed the purification with the formula, “O Agni, lord of vows,” he places a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula, “I shall perform the vow; may I be capable of it; may it be successful for me, svāhā!”

3.1.3.43. He breathes out and breathes in, having filled himself from within with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), saying: "Here I go from untruth to truth. 3.1.3.44. "Untruth, indeed, belongs to humans; truth belongs to the gods. Thus he goes from among humans to the gods. So indeed did the gods enter upon their vow, so did the seers (*ṛṣi*), so did those ancient Vedic scholars who were seekers of the Truth (*ṛtāyu*). Thus they say: "Just as for those who have been excluded by the *yajus* formula, there would be either a loss of vitality or a destruction [of the rite], so a penance (*prāyaścitti*) must be performed."
3.1.3.45. Having brought a branch with a *yajus* formula at evening itself, he drives away the calves with a *yajus* formula.
3.1.3.46. Indeed, in the morning, he undertakes the vow for the sake of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 3.1.3.47. He remains restrained in speech until the conclusion of the rite.
3.1.3.48. Regarding this they say: "Who is worthy [to perform the sacrifice]—one who has entered upon the vow (*vrata*) and is restrained in speech, or one who speaks much while speaking the truth?

3.1.3.49. Whatever one who has not entered upon the vow might do with the *yajus* formulas, that is just as if one were to officiate for someone who has not been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) or for one who has not entered upon the vow.

3.1.3.50. There are indeed three ways of entering upon the vow for the New and Full Moon sacrifices: after having piled the sacred fires (*anvāhāryapacana*), with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and with the calves.
3.1.3.51. Now, one [view] is that [the *iṣṭi* should be performed] "when the sacrificial oblations have been set down.

3.1.3.52. Just as rice and barley would be scattered from a cart whose fastenings have come loose, even so, for one who has not entered upon the vow, whatever is performed with a *yajus* formula is scattered; it is as if the *iṣṭi* itself were being led away. There is no mental *iṣṭi*, nor is there an *upavasatha* day for the *iṣṭi*.
3.1.3.53. That [position] collapses because of the words: "when the sacrificial oblations have been set down."

3.2.1.1. Now, therefore, he consecrates the oblation while it is being poured out with the mantra: “I invoke here Agni the Hotṛ; I invoke the gods for this my oblation. 3.2.1.2. Regarding this, they say: “One should consecrate the oblation while it is being poured out with ‘I invoke Agni the Hotṛ here’; then, when the officiating priests have approached, one should say ‘May the gods come, well-disposed’; and when they are departing again, one should say ‘May the gods depart from this my oblation. This is the deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*).”
3.2.1.3. With the entire [formula], he should consecrate the oblation itself as it is being poured out.

3.2.1.4. While the mortar and pestle and the lower and upper grinding stones are being joined, [he recites]: "Ka joins you; may he join you. 3.2.1.5. [He recites]: "The potsherds which [are used] in the *gharma*—the wise ones pile them up; they belong to Pūṣan’s vow; may Indra and Vāyu join them."
3.2.1.6. Having recited this very same [formula], at the time of release, he says: "May Indra and Vāyu release [it]. 3.2.1.7.

Now, therefore, regarding the case of a *kapāla* that has been lost. 3.2.1.8. On this point there is indeed a Brāhmaṇa passage: "If one *kapāla* should be lost, one month of the year remains unfulfilled; [therefore, one should offer] a cake on one *kapāla* to Heaven and Earth."
3.2.1.9. Regarding this, they say: "If there should be a loss of this expiatory offering (prāyaścitti-yā iṣṭi), then no expiation would remain.

3.2.1.10. One should offer a spoonful (sruvāhuti) into the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "The thirty-three threads which have been stretched out—this I establish; svāhā! 3.2.1.11. Then one replaces it with another, [with the mantra]: "May the Gharma reach the gods," if [the original] has already been placed.
3.2.1.12. Now, if [the vessel] should break while being taken away, one should offer this very same oblation: "Thirty-three threads—svāhā! The heated offering (gharma) shall go to the gods—svāhā!
3.2.1.13. Now, therefore, concerning a broken potsherd. 3.2.1.14. If it should break before it has been sprinkled with water, one should fetch another and then proceed with the rite.

3.2.1.15. Now, if that which has been sprinkled should break, one should offer a spoonful of oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: “The *gharma* is unbroken, O giver of vigor; may they follow along with life, *svāhā*! 3.2.1.16. Then he replaces it with another, saying: “Even without a bond, before the breaking and the bursting asunder, Maghavan, the restorer, shall join the fracture; he shall put back together what was torn apart. 3.2.1.17. Then he throws this [piece] into the ashes.

3.2.1.18. Now, therefore, regarding vessels that have cracked. 3.2.1.19. If one should crack while it has not yet been sprinkled with water, one should fetch another and then proceed with the ritual. 3.2.1.20.
But if it should crack while it has already been sprinkled with water, one should use whichever vessel cracks sooner.

3.2.1.21. Upon that [fire], he should offer a spoonful of oblation either on the *gārhapatya* or the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse: “The grey-haired one has swallowed the youth who was running about in the assembly of many; behold the wisdom of the god through his greatness! Today the conqueror has died, the same as before—*svāhā!*” (TĀ 4.20.1). 3.2.1.22. Then he sets another [fire] in its place with the verse: “Even without a binding, before the devourers have torn it apart, the bountiful Maghavan, the lord of the house, is the restorer of the breach; he shall repair what was shattered again. (RV 6.47.7)
3.2.1.23. If it is made of wood, he strikes it with something else that is after it; and if it is made of clay, he simply pushes it away with ashes.
3.2.1.24. Now, therefore, regarding the spilt *sānnāyya* offering.

3.2.2.1. Now, therefore, having poured a water-pot over the *sānnāyya* that has been spilled, he should consecrate it with the formula: “To the Lord of the Earth, svāhā! To the Lord of the World, svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, svāhā! 3.2.2.2.
If there should be enough for the performance, he should proceed with the ritual. 3.2.2.3.
If a continuous supply should remain, he should silently pour more in and proceed.

3.2.2.4. Now, if everything should spill out, one should have the *sāṃnāyya* milked according to the procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*. 3.2.2.5. Now, if everything should break, having offered the oblation with the verse, “The quivering, running away,” and having replaced it with the verse, “Even without a bond,” one should have the *sāṃnāyya* milked according to the very same procedure for the *sāṃnāyya*. 3.2.2.6. Now, if impurity should enter it, or if a dog should drink from it.

3.2.2.7. If a black bird or a monkey should alight [on the milk], one should carry it away, wash the vessel, and after having it cleansed, have the *sānnāyya* milked according to the procedure for the *sānnāyya*.
3.2.2.8. Hastin, the son of Gathuna Ārkṣākāyaṇa, drank the *sānnāyya*.
3.2.2.9. He used to walk about in a state of agitation, saying, "O men, had you known this, the elephant would have drunk our *sānnāyya*; we would have prescribed an expiation for him."

3.2.2.10. Regarding this, Uddālaka Āruṇi said: "Alpa-maryā Gāglana was distressed when he did not know this much: 'The expiation for a sacrifice is indeed the ritual procedure for the *sānnāyya* offering; the ritual procedure for the *sānnāyya* is the ritual procedure for the *agnihotra*; [the expiation] for the *agnihotra* is [the same]. One should milk the *sānnāyya* according to the ritual procedure for the *sānnāyya*. 3.2.2.11. He milks the *sānnāyya* according to the very ritual procedure for the *sānnāyya*. 3.2.2.12. Now, therefore, regarding the spilling of the clarified butter (*ājya*) itself.
3.2.2.13. Now, some indeed pour together this *svadhā* [offering], saying: "I pour thee with the *yajus*, O *san*. This is a point for deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*). 3.2.2.14.
Having poured out a vessel of water, he should instead consecrate it with this mantra: "To Bhūpati, *svāhā*! 3.2.2.15.
If there should be enough for the performance, he should perform it.

3.2.2.16. If a remnant of the continuity should remain, one should silently pour more [milk] on top and proceed with the rite. 3.2.2.17. Now, if the entire [milk] should spill out, one should fetch another [portion], pour it out, and then proceed with the rite.

3.2.2.18. Now, if the entire [milk] should break [or leak], having offered the oblation with the verse, "The trembling one who runs away," and having replaced it with the verse, "Whatever [is done] even without attachment," one should fetch another [portion], pour it out, and then proceed with the rite.
3.2.2.19. Now, if that which has been drawn should spill, one should pour water into it and consecrate it with this mantra: "To Bhūpati, svāhā! 3.2.2.20.
If there should be enough for the performance, one should proceed with the rite.
3.2.2.21. If a continuous supply should remain, one should silently pour more in and proceed.
3.2.2.22. Now, if the entire [milk] should spill over, one should take it up with the *yajus*-formulas belonging to that [cow] from which it spilled.

3.2.2.23. Now, if the entire [vessel] should break, having offered the oblation with the verse, "The trembling one who runs away," and having replaced it with the verse, "Whatever [is done] even apart from attachment," one should take it up with the *yajus*-formulas belonging to that very same [cow].
3.2.2.24. Now, therefore, regarding the opening for the clarified butter (*ājyāvakāśa*).
3.2.2.25. He looks at it, saying: "Thou art ghee; thou art truth. 3.2.2.26.

Now, some indeed purify the ghee without looking at it. If one were to do so, he would purify only the ghee, not himself. 3.2.2.27. But when he purifies it after having looked at it, he purifies himself by means of the ghee, and the ghee by means of the two strainers.
3.2.2.28. Therefore, one should purify [the butter] only after having inspected it.
3.2.2.29. Now, therefore, regarding the very taking of the portions of clarified butter (ājyagraha).

3.2.2.30. Now, some indeed set aside those portions of clarified butter belonging to the cake-offering (pauroḍāśika), and they take them with the sacrificial formulas belonging to the sacrificer (yājamānayajus).

3.2.2.31. The *pauroḍāśika* formulas are indeed the womb; the *ājyagraha* formulas are the self; and the *yājamāna-yajus* formulas are the seed. 3.2.2.32. If he were to act in this manner [by using the *yājamāna-yajus* for the *ājyagrahas*], he would place his own self elsewhere than in the womb; that would be just like that. 3.2.2.33. The Adhvaryu should take [the *ājyagrahas*] with the *pauroḍāśika* formulas, and the sacrificer should recite the *yājamāna-yajus* formulas [over them]. Just as one would pour semen into the womb, so does he place his own self in the womb; that is just like that.
3.2.2.34. He consecrates the [ghee] being taken into the *juhū* ladle with: "O you who belong to the five...
"I take you for the restraint of the five winds, for the restraint of the five peoples, and for support. Thus.
3.2.3.2. If there are five portions, he takes the fifth with the formula, "For desire thee. 3.2.3.3. Or, at the fourth portion, he may optionally follow the same formula.

3.2.3.4. Then, in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he takes [the butter] with the formula, "For the chariot of the five-holed [sacrificial post], for the distinction, for the support and the upholder, I take thee."
3.2.3.5. If there are five portions, he takes the fifth with the formula: “For desire thee” (TS 1.6.13.1.2). 3.2.3.6. Or, he may optionally apply the formula for desire at the fourth portion.
3.2.3.7. Then, in the *upabhṛt* ladle itself, he takes [the portions] with the formulas: “I take thee for good heroism” and “I take thee for excellent Brahman-splendor.”
3.2.3.8. He takes the fifth [portion] with "For desire thee," if there are five portions.
3.2.3.9. Or he may optionally follow it through the fourth [verse].
3.2.3.10. Then, regarding the *dhruvā* [ladle], he says: "Bhūḥ! I take [this] oblation for us from the deities."
3.2.3.11. If there are five portions, he recites the fifth [verse], "For desire, thee.
3.2.3.12. Or, at the fourth [portion], he may optionally follow [the verse] for desire.

3.2.3.13. Then he consecrates the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) as they are being laid down: with the formula "Thou art firm; may I be firm among my kinsmen," he addresses the middle enclosing-stick; with "And thou art a watcher, a finder of wealth," and "Thou art fierce; may I be fierce among my kinsmen," the southern one; with "And thou art a watcher, a finder of wealth," and "Thou art overpowering; may I be overpowering among my kinsmen," the northern one; and with "And thou art a watcher, a finder of wealth."

3.2.3.14. Then, having taken hold of the middle enclosing-stick (paridhi), he mutters: "I yoke thee with the sacred word (*brahman*)... O Agni, we weave for thee. 3.2.3.15. As the grass-bundle (*prastara*) is being placed down, he says over the ladles (*sruc*) that have been set down: "O Agni, whatever of this sacrifice of mine... in thy lap; Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ. 3.2.3.16.
Then he consecrates the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) that have been set down and the fuel-wood (*idhma*) being added: "O Agni, kindled by the gods, kindled by the wise, thou of lovely tongue..."

3.2.3.17. Regarding this, they say: "One should recite the mantra over the fuel-stick (*idhma*) as it is being placed on the fire: 'O Agni, kindled by the gods, kindled by wisdom... and "one should look at the Hotṛ priest with the words 'O sweet-tongued one' (*mandrajihva*). This is the deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*). 3.2.3.18.
With the entire formula, he recites the mantra over the fuel-stick as it is being placed on the fire.
3.2.3.19. While the grass-broom (*veda*) is being swept across it, he recites: "O Agni, be a source of prosperity for the sacrificer; [drive away] those who seek to harm us."
3.2.3.20. While the *āghāra* libation is being poured with the *sruva* ladle, he recites: "Thou art the mind, belonging to Prajāpati; enter me with the mind that is existence. 3.2.3.21.
With the two *sruc* ladles, for the subsequent libation, he recites: "Thou art speech, belonging to Indra, [conquering] rivals. 3.2.3.22.
While the *pravara* (the choosing of the Hotṛ) is being performed, he recites: "O immortal Hotṛ, it conquers upon thy head for the increase of wealth, for good progeny, and for heroic vigor."
3.2.3.23. He consecrates each *prayāja* offering as it is offered with: "I gratify Vasant, the first of the seasons; may those two, being gratified, gratify me. 3.2.3.24.
Both *ājyabhāga* offerings, having been offered, [he consecrates them] with: "Through the sacrifice to Agni and Soma today, may I become possessed of sight.
3.2.3.25. [He consecrates] the oblation for Agni with: "Through the sacrifice to Agni today, may I become an eater of food."
3.2.3.26. "Thou art unerring; may I become unerring; may I not be deceived by such-and-such"—with these words, he performs the *upāṃśuyāja*.
3.2.3.27. "By the sacrifice to Agni and Soma today, may I become a slayer of Vṛtra"—with these words, he performs the *agnīṣomīya* offering.
3.2.3.28. "By the sacrifice to Indra and Agni today, may I become possessed of power and an eater of food"—with these words, he performs the *aindrāgna* offering.
3.2.3.29. “Through the sacrifice to Indra on this day, may I become possessed of power,” thus for the offering to Indra.
3.2.3.30. “Through the sacrifice to Mahendra on this day, may I attain victory and greatness,” thus if one is a sacrificer to Mahendra.
3.2.3.31. “Through the sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt on this day, may I, long-lived, attain a firm foundation through the sacrifice,” thus for the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt.
Now, therefore, he consecrates the *prāśitra* portion as it is being cut off with: “May Agni protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings; may Savitṛ grant me victory. 3.3.1.2.
As the *iḍā* is being brought forward, [he recites]: “O thou of beautiful form and rain-like color, come hither! Come toward these auspicious dwellings—Sarasvatī, come!”

3.3.1.3. While the intermediate *iḍā* is being cut off, [he recites]: "Thou art delight; thou art rest; thou art the noble one. 3.3.1.4. While that very same [portion] is being invoked in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), [he recites]: "O beloved one, may I share in thy belovedness; O invited one, may I share in thy invitation. 3.3.1.5. While it is being invoked aloud (*uccais*), [he recites]: "May this be my true blessing; O invited one, may I share in thy invitation."

3.3.1.6. Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "When the Hotṛ invokes the *iḍā*, then the sacrificer, looking at the Hotṛ, should meditate on Vāyu with his mind; he releases the calf to its mother. (C.p.39) 3.3.1.7.

When he recognizes the words "The *iḍā* has been invoked," then he meditates on Vāyu with his mind, saying: "Vāyu is your calf; I release him to you. With Vāyu as your calf, O Faith, milk for me through austerity that [desired object] over there. (N1,33a2)

3.3.1.8. Whatever desire he may wish for, that very desire is fulfilled for him. 3.3.1.9. Having prepared a cake on eight potsherds for Barhiṣad, he recites over the *anvāhārya* rice: "O Bradhna, overflow! Over the *saṃtati* oblation being offered, he says: "Thou art the portion of Prajāpati. Over the *anūyāja* sacrifice that has been performed, he says: "May the mind, as light, enjoy [the offering]. 3.3.1.10. He consecrates the sacrifice with the formula: "Through the sacrifice to the gods by means of the *barhis*, may I attain a firm foundation through the sacrifice."

3.3.1.11. Then he separates the two offering-spoons (*srucau*) with the two *vājavatī* verses: “By the impulse of strength (*vāja*), may I win both the upward-grasp (*udgrābha*) and the downward-grasp (*nigrābha*).

3.3.1.12. Now, when the Hotṛ begins the *ujjitī* formulas, he consecrates them according to the respective deities: “May I follow and win the victory of Agni; may I follow and win the victory of Soma... may I follow and win the victory of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. 3.3.1.13. There is indeed a Brāhmaṇa passage: “This is one milking of the sacrifice, and another is in the *iḍā*; at that very time, he should say: ‘These blessings have come, desiring to be milked.’”
3.3.1.14. When he recognizes [the formula], "This sacrificer, so-and-so, desires," he mutters: "O, these blessings have come—progeny and food. 3.3.1.15.
As the *prastara* is being thrown into the fire, [he says]: "May Agni, as the deity, lead you by means of a red [horse]; may Sūrya, as the deity, lead you. 3.3.1.16.

At this point, if the sacrificer has gone away on a journey, he should throw the sacrificer’s portion into the fire together with the *prastara*, saying: "The world named Vibhān belongs to Prajāpati; therein I place you, together with the sacrificer."
3.3.1.17. If he were to say, “Together with the sacrificer,” the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely.
3.3.1.18. But there is indeed a Brāhmaṇa passage: “This world of Prajāpati is named Vibhān; verily, he places him therein together with the sacrificer. 3.3.1.19.
Therefore, one may certainly say, “Together with the sacrificer,” and one may certainly say, “That world of the sacrificer.”
3.3.1.20. Now, as the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are being thrown into the fire, [he recites]: "I release you from the fetters" (3.3.2).
"I release you from the fetters, O you who hold your portions among the deities. (N1,33a9; 1081B 113; M97)
3.3.2.2. At the *śaṃyuvāka*, he says: "O Viṣṇu, through the sacrifice and the worship of the gods on this day of peace (*śaṃyu*), may I attain a firm foundation.

3.3.2.3. Then, over the *veda* grass-bundle, he recites according to the meter: "Thou art the *veda*, thou art acquisition; may I acquire. May the *veda* grant me vigor. 3.3.2.4. Over the *veda* grass-bundle, he says: "Thou art the *veda*, thou art acquisition; may I acquire. May I eat of such-and-such," and he should utter the name of whatever he covets from his rival. By doing so, he seizes all of that from him.
3.3.2.5. “May the Veda grant us nourishment accompanied by ghee, provided with a nest, thousandfold, and full of vigor,” so says the Anubrāhmaṇa.

3.3.2.6. Regarding the Veda: “Thou art the Veda; thou art acquisition; may I acquire what is good. Thou art gain; thou art the winner; may I win. [I win] offspring, cattle, and the heavenly world. Thou art action; thou art the doer of action. May the Veda grant us nourishment accompanied by ghee, provided with a nest, thousandfold, and full of vigor.
3.3.2.7. Then, remaining seated right there, he performs the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings in succession.

3.3.2.8. He recites the consecratory formulas over the offerings: with the verse for Soma, "Through the sacrifice to the gods of Soma, may I, possessing good seed, deposit seed"; with the verse for Tvaṣṭṛ, "Through the sacrifice to the gods of Tvaṣṭṛ, may I produce the form of cattle"; and for both subsequent offerings, "The wives of the gods, Agni the master of the house—may I through the sacrifice to the gods of this pair, by means of this union, become prolific.
3.3.2.9. Then, having gone forward to the east, he causes the *dhruvā* ladle to swell with the formula, "May the *dhruvā* swell with clarified butter."
3.3.2.10. Then he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* with the verse, “O gods, you who know the way.
3.3.2.11. At this point, he should throw the sacrificer’s portion into the fire if they should forget it there, saying, “The world of Prajāpati is named Vibhān.
3.3.2.12. Then, having placed the *praṇītā* waters within the altar and sitting down to the south, he consumes the sacrificer’s portion.
3.3.2.13. “This is offered for one who has undertaken a vow,” they say; “for thus he becomes one who has partaken of the sacrifice within. 3.3.2.14.

Then, having sipped water and stepped down, he touches the full vessel with the formula: “Thou art being; mayest thou become being for me. 3.3.2.15. Then he purifies the quarters with the formula: “May the gods and the officiating priests purify themselves in the eastern quarter.”

3.3.2.16. Then he pours water into his joined palms with a triplet [of verses], beginning: "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss... (RV X.9.1). 3.3.2.17. Then he wipes himself with two verses, beginning: "O Indra, unite me with wealth; unite me with splendor... (VS XXXIV.50–51). 3.3.2.18. Then, having risen, he strides the Viṣṇu-strides along the southern edge of the altar.

3.3.2.19. Stepping down toward the northern shoulder of the altar, he places his right foot forward first and steps out following with the left, saying: "O Viṣṇu, this is your stride, the slayer of the adversary. 3.3.2.20.
Now, some indeed perform this stepping toward the altar with the fourth turn.

3.3.2.21. The altar is indeed the sacrificer’s station (*yajamānāyatana*). If someone were to say of him there, “He has been displaced from his station; he will not remain established,” it would surely come to pass exactly so. Therefore, on the third step itself, he should follow through with a fourth, or he should drag it along the forepart of the foot, saying: “O Viṣṇu, you are a stride; you are the slayer of those who act as enemies. 3.3.2.22. Then he strides forward toward the east, saying: “We have gone to the light; we have gone to the light” (ŚB 1.6.6a). 3.3.2.23. Then he worships the sun.
3.3.3.1. Then he worships the sun with the mantra: “May I not be severed from your sight; may I become one with light” (TS 1.6.6b–e).
3.3.3.2. He turns back toward the right with the mantra: “I turn following the turning of Indra” (TS 1.6.6f).

3.3.3.3. At that very moment he turns back [toward the fire], saying: "May I be united with offspring; may offspring be united with me. 3.3.3.4. Then he adds fuel, saying: "O Agni, being kindled, shine for me.
3.3.3.5. Then he pays homage, saying: "May the sacrifice be rich in wealth; may I become more wealthy."

3.3.3.6. Then, with two *āgnipāvamānī* verses, he approaches the *gārhapatya* fire: "O Agni, you purify the lives... and "O Agni, purify yourself... (1.6.6 l-m). 3.3.3.7. Then he pays homage. 3.3.3.8. With the words "O Agni, lord of the house," he invokes blessings: "May I attain a hundred winters; I invoke this blessing for myself, for so-and-so, as one full of light. First, he pronounces his own name; then, in order, those of "so-and-so, so-and-so" for his sons, ending with the word "progeny."
3.3.3.9. With the mantra, “May *Ōkas* yoke you; may he release you” (TS 1.6.6.0), he gazes at the mortar and pestle. 3.3.3.10.

With the mantra, “The potsherds which [were used] for the *gharma*—those of the wise Pūṣan, may Indra and Vāyu release them as well for the sake of the vow” (TS 1.5.10 = 1.1.7.k), they collect the potsherds.
3.3.3.11. Then, by means of the re-seizing of the sacrifice, he goes forward to the east with the mantra, “The sacrifice has come into being; it has become manifest” (TS 1.6.6.3–4.q).
3.3.3.12. Then, having stepped forward toward the east, he mutters: "O Agni, may this sacrifice be rich in cattle, rich in sheep, and rich in horses" (TS 1.6.6.1).

3.3.3.13. Then he takes up the *upaveśa* grass-bundle. 3.3.3.14. He hides it in front of the *utkara* heap, pointing westward, from its thickest part, with the formula: "May he who seeks to diminish us find no hero-lord" (TS 3.7.6.14).

3.3.3.15. Then, standing to the south, he releases the vow with the formula: “Stepping forth again and again, Indra slew Vṛtra for the sake of prosperity,” so says the Brāhmaṇa. 3.3.3.16. With the formula, “The plants are full of milk,” he sips water through the filter with the formula, “Full of milk... unite” (1.5.10g). 3.3.3.17. Having performed the purification with the formula, “O Agni, Lord of the Vow,” he places a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula: “I shall perform the vow; I was able to do it; may that be successful for me, svāhā! (M99)
3.3.3.18. "He breathes out and breathes in. Having filled himself from within with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he says: "From truth (*satya*) I go unto immortality (*amṛta*).
3.3.3.19. The gods are indeed truth; the heavenly world (*suvarga loka*) is immortality. Thus, he goes from the gods to the heavenly world.

3.3.3.20. Then, having sat down to the south, he drinks the milk, saying: "May this oblation be productive for me—possessing ten heroes, with a complete retinue—for my well-being! May it win for me self, offspring, cattle, fearlessness, worlds, and rain! May Agni make my progeny abundant; bestow upon us food, milk, and seed! Thus he turns back.

3.3.3.21. Now, therefore, follows the Brāhmaṇa passage: "From the sacrifice, indeed, the sacrificer is born when he performs the sacrifice. Every half-month they consecrate him as one consisting of the Brahman, consisting of the sacrifice, consisting of the world, consisting of breath, and consisting of immortality. For one who is born is indeed dependent on milk; for one who is born, one does not offer boiled rice or parched grain flour. Indeed, one provides milk for the newborn. Just as a leather bag is empty and dried out when its contents have been sucked out, so indeed is he at this time."

The sacrifice, the sacrifice, is the sacrificer; the sacrificer is the moon. Indeed, the skin-bag is dried up and sucked empty by the milk; the sacrifice, having been dried up and sucked empty by his thought, causes it to swell again. When he drinks the milk, he thereby thinks of swelling the self, the sacrifice, and the moon. Therefore, one should drink the milk; one should drink the milk. 3.4 Āgrayaṇa 3.4.1 [K4,24a10-;1081B 116; ī 112 34b l.5]

3.4.1.1. One who is about to perform the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice procures new rice and millet. 3.4.1.2. Having sacrificed with the *āmāvāsya* oblation, he offers the following: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a millet pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a pap for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. 3.4.1.3. Once the offerings have been set out, he recites the *prāṇagraha* formulas and the *pṛśni* verses.

3.4.1.4. Having released his speech with the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he offers these [oblations] with four spoonfuls using the *Saptahotṛ* formula, ending with "svāhā. 3.4.1.5(?).
With the verse, "His fuel-sticks stand upright" (TS 4.1.8a), he offers the twelve *Āprī* oblations.
3.4.1.6. With the verse, "To him who has a hundred weapons, who has a hundred powers" (TS 5.7.2d), he offers the five *Ājyānī* oblations.
3.4.1.7. Or rather, the *hotṛ* himself is the thirtieth among these. 3.4.1.8. When the oblations have been cooked, he brings the *yajus* formula for the one possessing the oblation (*haviṣmant*).
3.4.1.9. He encloses the altar (*vedi*) and mutters the *karaṇa* formula.
3.4.1.10. The ritual action is accomplished until its completion.
3.4.1.11. When [the fire] is near [completion], he recites the *apānagrahas* and... he recites the *daśahotṛ*. 3.4.1.12.
He recites the *anuvākyā* for the fire being kindled.

3.4.1.13. He recites seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. 3.4.1.14. The ritual action is successfully accomplished up to the *prayāja* offerings. 3.4.1.15. Having performed the *prayāja* offerings, he consecrates them with the formula: "May my sacrifice and my progeny [prosper]."
3.4.1.16. He offers the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāgau*) with the formula: "And may all life, the heavenly world, and the Brahman and Kṣatra that grant my desires [be mine].
3.4.1.17. He recites: "Possessing wealth... [may he] attain wealth through the fire. 3.4.1.18.
He performs the offering with the *juṣāṇa* formula; he makes the libation when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
3.4.1.19. Saying, "Recite for Soma," while taking portions of the clarified butter itself, he recites [the invitatory verse]: "O you who are swelling with milk, the dispeller of disease... 3.4.1.20.
He performs the offering with the very same [verse] as it is being enjoyed; when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the oblation. 3.4.1.21.
Saying, "Recite for Agni," he speaks while spreading [the base] and cutting off [the portion].
3.4.1.22. He recites: "Agni is the head" (4.1.11c).
3.4.1.24. While spreading the underlayer and cutting the portions, he says: "Recite for Soma."
3.4.1.25. He recites: "O Soma, [flow] for us from every side. 3.4.1.26. He performs the offering with: "Those abodes of yours... At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation. 3.4.1.27.
Saying, "Recite for Indra and Agni," while spreading the under-layer and cutting the portions, he recites: "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven..."

3.4.1.28. He recites the offering verse, “He has pierced Vṛtra” (4.2.11b). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation. 3.4.1.29. While spreading the underlayer [of ghee] and cutting the portions, he says, “Recite for the Viśve Devas!
3.4.1.30. He recites the invitatory verse, “O Viśve Devas, increasers of Truth” (2.4.14q, 4.1.11p).
3.4.1.31. He offers with the verse: “O All-Gods, hear this invocation. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation. 3.4.1.32.
Saying, “Recite for Heaven and Earth,” he places the cake on one potsherd, which has been spread with butter and sprinkled with butter.
3.4.1.33. He recites after [the invitatory verse]: “May Heaven and Earth [protect] this [sacrifice] of ours.”
3.4.1.34. He performs the sacrifice with the mantra, "O you who were born first" (TS 1.6.2.1). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
3.4.1.35. With the mantra, "After the sacrifices," he consecrates the cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) once it has been offered.

3.4.2.1. He consecrates with the mantra “anu yajñaiḥ” the cake on one potsherd that has been offered, saying: “May we prosper through cattle, through horses, through all forms of nourishment, through offspring, and through power; may the gods lead our sacrifice straight forward.”

3.4.2.2. If it should turn over, having set it upright and offered with the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*, he should offer with the two subsequent [verses]: "May you be established through sacrifices, through wealth, through horses, through all prosperity, through offspring, and through sensory power; may Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable, protect us from all misfortunes within with well-being, Svāhā! May your strengths, may your words, may your milks, may your heights, and may your joints come to you at every joint, O Sacrifice, Svāhā!"—thus.
3.4.2.3. Reciting, “For Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, after [the offering], svāhā!,” he spreads an underlayer of ghee while cutting portions.
3.4.2.4. He cuts a portion once from the northern half of each of all the oblations.
3.4.2.5. Having cut a portion from the single-pot-sherd cake from its receptacle, he pours ghee over it twice.
3.4.2.6. He does not anoint [the two spoons]. 3.4.2.7. He recites as the two *saṃyājyā* verses two *gāyatrī* verses: “O Agni, awaken with a hymn” (4.1.11t). 3.4.2.8.
He performs the offering with the verse: “He is the bearer of oblations” (4.1.11u).
3.4.2.9. He makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
3.4.2.10. Having stepped across and set [the vessels] down in their respective places, he cuts off the *prāśitra*.
3.4.2.11. Having touched water, he cuts off the *iḍā*.
3.4.2.12. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places [the portion] for the *āgnīdhra*.
3.4.2.13. They consume [the portions]; they purify themselves; they carry [the *iḍā*] around. 3.4.2.14.
When the *prāśitra* has been consumed by the *brahman*, the *āgnīdhra* sits down at the rubbish heap (*utkara*) with a water-pot.
3.4.2.15. He gives a garment; he gives the first-born calf. To him for whom there is the *āgrayaṇa* offering, he gives *khārīs* [of grain].
3.4.2.16. Following the continuity, he offers the oblation for the *hotṛ*.
3.4.2.17. The ritual proceeds successfully up to the *patnī-homa*.

3.4.2.18. Following the *patnīhoma*, he offers two oblations with the *sruva*-ladle, saying: “Thou art the messenger of the year, the image [of it]... (VS 28.36). 3.4.2.19. The *saumya* rite is successfully completed. 3.4.2.20.

Having placed together portions of the other sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*), he sits down to the south and eats his portion of the sacrificer’s share three times, saying: “The gods have led us from good to better” (VS 5.7.2h,1; B2.4.8.7,1), and “By thee, O pleasant one, in this dwelling... (ibid. 2).
3.4.2.21. "The rite is accomplished; it is concluded. Thus ends the fourth section (anuvāka).
3.5–6. The Office of the Brahman.

The Brahman priest, having been chosen, puts on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), sips water, and takes the fire into himself with two verses: "I first take the fire into myself; that fire of ours which is within our hearts, O fathers" (TS 5.7.9a).

3.5.1.2. He touches [the post] with his hand, saying: “May I be able for the sake of the work and for the gods; for the sake of power and for the sake of good action. 3.5.1.3. Saying, “Bṛhaspati is the Brahman,” he steps between the altar and the rubbish-heap (utkara).

3.5.1.4. Saying, “May he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me, may he protect the rule of the sacrifice,” he steps across the rear of the altar and says, “Daidhiṣavyā.”

3.5.1.5. He takes a blade of grass from where he is about to sit down, with the mantra: “Arise from here; sit on the seat of another, you who are more cooked than we. 3.5.1.6. With the mantra, “Parāvasu is cast out,” he throws away the blade of grass. 3.5.1.7. Having made a lap with the mantra, “Here I sit upon the seat of life,” he sits down.

3.5.1.8. Having sat down, he mutters: "O God Savitṛ, this [man] chooses you, Bṛhaspati, the divine Brahman. Declare that to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī; the Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh to the Paṅkti; the Paṅkti to the Vasus; the Vasus to the Rudras; the Rudras to the Ādityas; the Ādityas to the Viśve Devas; the Viśve Devas to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati to the Brahman. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Bṛhaspati!"
"I am the Brahmā of the gods; let him among men reach me who would either deceive me or seek to examine me: *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar*, *oṃ*, I am such-and-such a man. 3.5.1.9.
While the *praṇītā* waters are being brought forward, he should restrain his speech until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*).
3.5.1.10. When [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Brahman, I shall bring forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech," [he should do so].

3.5.1.11. He pronounces this [formula]: “Lead forth the sacrifice; prosper these deities! May the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament, where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is; there, place this sacrifice and the sacrificer! Oṃ, lead forth! 3.5.1.12. While the *stambayajus* is being carried away from the northern enclosure-line (*parigraha*). 3.5.1.13.
When he says, “O Brahman, I shall perform the northern enclosure-line,” [the Brahman responds].

3.5.1.14. He impels it [the sacrificer] with: “O Bṛhaspati, encompass the altar; may it be dear to the gods. May it be pleasant; strew the sacrificial grass within its lap. May the lap of Aditi be auspicious for us; encompass it! 3.5.1.15.

While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he restrains his speech until the concluding formula (*paridhāna*). 3.5.1.16. While each *puro’nuvākyā* verse is being recited, he restrains his speech until the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
3.5.1.17. Whenever he performs [a rite] with either a *ṛc* or a *yajus*, he restrains his speech until the concluding recitation (*paridhāna*).

3.5.1.18. If he were to release his speech in the interval, he would sever the sacrifice. 3.5.1.19. Now, if he should release it through negligence, he should recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: “O Viṣṇu, you who are nearest to us, grant us protection, O Conqueror! Your streams, dripping with honey, flow forth like inexhaustible wells” (TS 3.1.10k).
3.5.1.20. While the *prāśitra* portion is being cut off, he restrains his speech.
While the *prāśitra* is being cut off, he restrains his speech until the impulse (*prasava*).
3.5.2.2 When he offers him the *prāśitra* portion, he touches water and gazes at it, saying: "I gaze upon you with the eye of Sūrya.
3.5.2.3 He receives it, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you.
3.5.2.4 He sets it down, saying: "I set you down in the lap of the Earth."
3.5.2.5. Regarding these two, some indeed consume [the remains]. Disregarding that [other view], one should consume from these two alone with the formula: "I consume thee with the mouth of Agni."

3.5.2.6. Having sprinkled [the vessel] with water and having passed over the teeth, he washes these [remnants] toward that direction while passing in front of the right knee, [reciting]: “By the belly of the Brāhmaṇa, by the sacred word of Bṛhaspati. Having poured them out and rinsed the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel, and having placed the portion for the Brahman priest into it, he cleanses it with water and touches his vital organs, [reciting]: “May speech be in my mouth; may smell be in my nose; may strength be in my thighs; may speed be in my knees; may my limbs be unharmed... do not harm me” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.7.2).

3.5.2.7. When he says, “O Brahman, we shall set forth,” and having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he gives the impulse with the words, “O Āgnīdhra, cleanse the fire once each [time]! (ĀpŚS 21.8). Then he says: “O God Savitṛ, this you have declared; impel it and perform the sacrifice! Bṛhaspati is the Brahman priest (3.1.7a,b); may he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me, O master of the sacrifice! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ! Be established! (3.5.2.7). 3.5.2.8. As for that which is not allotted [to him], he should remain restrained in speech... if he were to speak much, he would cut the sacrifice asunder.
3.5.2.9. When he restrains his speech at each sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), he becomes one whose deity is the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*). He does not interrupt the sacrifice. 3.5.2.10.

Once the *samiṣṭayajus* oblation has been offered, having gone out by the same way he came, he throws two wood-shavings (*śakala*) into the *āhavanīya* fire with the mantra: "Whatever injury has occurred to my self, Agni has restored my sight. 3.5.2.11.
By this very [procedure], one becomes the *brahmán* priest for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the *iṣṭi*s, the *cāturmāsya*s, and the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*).

3.5.2.12. Wherever they carry the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) around for him, he touches water there and awaits it with his mind alone; thus he receives it with his mind, thus he eats it with his mind and his breath, and thus, having touched water, he mentally touches his vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Thus ends the fifth section (*anuvāka*).
By this very same [formula], the Brahman [priest] [addresses] the Dīkṣaṇīyā [offering]: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite for the Gharma.
3.6.1.2. Having uttered the Divākīrtyā verse, the Brahman gives the impulse (prasauti).

3.6.1.3. Now, when he carries the *mahāvīra* vessel eastward, the Brahman priest follows along behind it from the south and performs his duties while standing to the south. 3.6.1.4. By this very same procedure, he becomes the Brahman for the *upasad* rites. When the *stambayajus* is being carried away from the great altar (*mahāvedi*), he sits to the south; likewise, he sits to the south of the altar as it is being prepared. 3.6.1.5. He goes to the south of the fire as it is being led forward and sits to the south of the northern enclosing line (*parigraha*). He goes to the south of the two *havirdhāna* carts as they are being drawn forward.

3.6.1.6. He stands to the south of the *audumbarī* post as it is being raised, and to the south of the *uparava* holes as they are about to be dug. Having placed the King (Soma) on his lap, he sits to the south while the *vaisarjana* offerings are being sacrificed. 3.6.1.7. He goes to the south of Agni and Soma as they are being led forth; before the fire is settled, he goes around the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth and stands to the south.
3.6.1.8. Once the fire has been settled, they go forward toward the east.
3.6.1.9. Having handed over the King [Soma] to the *adhvaryu*, and having sat down to the right of the *havirdhāna* shed, he remains seated to the south of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
3.6.1.10. While the *vasatīvarī* waters are being carried around, he stands to the south at the *āgnīdhra* shed; they dwell together there.

3.6.1.11. When they awaken him for the *prātaranuvāka*, he puts on the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavīta*), sips water, and having taken the fire into himself with two verses, enters in this very manner... Having gone by the front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds and behind the *āhavanīya* fire, he sits down in front of the southern *havirdhāna*. Once the *prātaranuvāka* has been commenced, he restrains his speech until the concluding formula.

3.6.1.12. When the morning recitation (*prātaranuvāka*) has been concluded, having entered the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door and having gone around the north of the *dhruva* vessel, he sits to the south of the king while the [Soma] is being pressed, and to the south of the cups as they are being drawn. 3.6.1.13. When, having drawn the cups, they proceed toward the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, 3.6.1.14. then, following after the *udgātṛ*s, the *brahmā* offers a spoonful of oblation with the verse: "O Bṛhaspati..."
3.6.2.1. “O Bṛhaspati, that which belongs to the enemy... O wonderful one! Svāhā!”—thus [he recites].
3.6.2.2. Then, having moved northward for the *bahis-pavamāna*, [they proceed].
3.6.2.3. When he says, "O Brahman, we shall chant; O Praśāstṛ," [the latter] says, "O Prastotṛ, O God Savitṛ, he has announced this to you.

3.6.2.4. The Brahman mutters the *prasava* formula: "Impel that, impel the sacrifice; Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Praise with long life! In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, praise accompanied by Indra! He utters aloud: "Thou art a ray; for habitation thee, quicken habitation!"—this mentally.

3.6.2.5. After the *bahiṣpavamāna* has been chanted, having returned by the same way he came and sat down in front of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he sits to the south of the animal for the *savanīya* offering.
3.6.2.6. Having offered its omentum and performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), they proceed together.
3.6.2.7. The procedure for proceeding together is well known.

3.6.2.8. Having gone north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, south of the *āgnīdhra*, and north of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, and having circumambulated the *sadas* to the north, he looks at the two doors of the *sadas* with the formula, "O divine doors, do not burn me," as he is about to enter the *sadas* by the western door.

3.6.2.9. He gazes at the *sadas* with the words, "Homage to the *sadas*"; he gazes at the sacrificer with the words, "Homage to the lord of the *sadas*"; he gazes at the eyes of those who have already entered from the east with the words, "Homage to the eyes of the friends who go before"; and [he gazes] with the words, "Homage to heaven, homage to earth."

3.6.2.10. Having gone to the west of the *audumbarī* post, he likewise throws away a blade of grass from the southern half of the *sadas*. He likewise sits down. Having sat down, he mutters [the following]. 3.6.2.11.
When the *pavamāna* chants have been introduced, he restrains his speech until the *paridhānīyā* verse; for the other *stotra*s and *śastra*s, it is until the *vaṣaṭ*-call. 3.6.2.12.
"Whenever he performs an action with a *ṛc* or a *yajus*, there he restrains his speech"—this is the same deliberation [as before]. (C.p. 45)

3.6.2.13. By this very [method] he becomes the Brahman priest for the morning pressing, by this for the midday pressing, and by this for the third pressing. 3.6.2.14. When they go down to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he follows them from the south and stands to the south while they perform the rites. 3.6.2.15. By this very [method] he becomes the Brahman priest for the concluding offering (udayanīya).
3.6.2.16. By this [same rule], the *anūbandhya* and the *udavasāna* [rites are explained].

3.6.2.17. If the sacrifice should fail through a lapse in the *ṛc*, he should say, "Announce it to the *brahman*. 3.6.2.18. If it fails through the *yajus* or if it fails through the *sāman*, he should likewise say, "Announce it to the *brahman*."
3.6.2.19. If the sacrifice should suffer a failure on account of the *ṛc*, one should offer a spoonful (*sruvāhuti*) at the Āgnīdhra fire with the words, “*bhūs svāhā*.
3.6.2.20. If [the failure] is on account of the *yajus*, one should offer a spoonful at the very same Āgnīdhra fire with the words, “*bhuvas svāhā*.
3.6.2.21. If [the failure] is on account of the *sāman*, one should offer a spoonful at the very same Āgnīdhra fire with the words, “*suvaḥ svāhā*.”

3.6.2.22. Now, if the sacrifice should fail from any cause whatsoever, or if it is unknown from where this has arisen, one should melt clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire, purify it, cleanse both the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles, hold a fuel-stick right there, seat a Brāhmaṇa to the south, go eastward, place [the offering] upon grass or a bundle of grass, lay on a fuel-stick, and offer into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "May the mind, as light, enjoy the clarified butter; may it unite this unimpaired sacrifice."
"May Bṛhaspati extend this [sacrifice] for us; may all the gods rejoice here—bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! (3.6.2.23).
This is the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitti) (3.6.2.24).
He who knows this is indeed the Brahman priest; therefore, one should appoint only such a person as the Brahman priest.

3.6.2.25. By this very [method], one becomes the Brahman priest for the Agniṣṭoma; by this for the Ukthya; by this for the Ṣoḍaśin; by this for the Atirātra; by this for the Āptoryāma; by this for the Vājapeya; by this for the Rājasūya; by this for the Arkāśvamedha; and by this for all sacrificial rites (yajñakratu). //15//
3.4 Āgrayaṇa 3.4.1.
One who is about to sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi procures fresh rice and śyāmāka grains.

3.4.1.2. Having sacrificed with the New Moon oblation, he offers [oblations] of old grain: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a porridge of *śyāmāka* millet for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, a porridge for the Viśve Devas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.
3.4.1.3. Once the grains have been poured out, he recites the *prāṇagraha* formulas and the *pṛśni* verses.
3.4.1.4. Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he [offers] with four ladlings to the *saptahotṛ* formula... ending with "svāhā. These [he offers].
3.4.1.5(?). "His kindling-sticks (*samidh*) are upright" (MS 4.1.8a)—with this, there are twelve *āprī* verses.
3.4.1.6. "To him whose weapons are a hundred, whose heroism is a hundred" (MS 5.7.2d)—with this, there are five *ājyānī* verses.
3.4.1.7. Or rather, the Hotṛ himself is the thirtieth of these.
3.4.1.8. When the oblations have been cooked, he recites the *yajus* for the one possessing oblations (*haviṣmant*).
3.4.1.9. He encloses the altar (*vedi*) and mutters the *karaṇa* formula. 3.4.1.10.
The ritual procedure is completed up until the formal setting down of the implements.

3.4.1.11. When [the fire] is near, he recites the *apānagraha* formulas... and he recites the *daśahotṛ*. 3.4.1.12. He recites the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the fire being kindled. 3.4.1.13. He recites seventeen kindling verses (*sāmidhenī*).
3.4.1.14. The ritual action is perfected up until the *prayāja* offerings.

3.4.1.15. Having performed the *prayāja* offerings, he consecrates them with the formula: "May my sacrifice and my offspring [be successful]. 3.4.1.16. With the formula, "All life and the heavenly world, and may my *brahman* and *kṣatra* be granters of desires," he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.
3.4.1.17. He recites: "May he obtain wealth through the four fires... (RV 10.127.1). 3.4.1.18.
He performs the sacrifice with the verse containing the word *juṣāṇa*; he offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
3.4.1.19. [The Adhvaryu says: "Recite for Soma! While taking the clarified butter, [the Hotṛ] recites: "Expansive like a cow, the dispeller of disease... (RV 10.127.2).

3.4.1.20. He performs the sacrifice while [the Adhvaryu] is indeed enjoying [the offering]; he offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. 3.4.1.21. While spreading [the butter] and cutting [the portions], he says, "Recite for Agni.
3.4.1.22. He recites, "Agni is the head... (RV 8.44.16).
(4.1.11d). 3.4.1.24. He says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Soma," while spreading [the base] and cutting [the portion].
3.4.1.25. He recites the response: "O Soma, [protect] us on every side" (4.1.11e).
3.4.1.26. He recites the verse, "Those abodes of yours... (VS 4.1.11f, etc.), and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. 3.4.1.27.
He says, "Recite for Indra and Agni," while spreading the underlayer of ghee and cutting the portions; he recites, "O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven...
(VS 4.2.11a). 3.4.1.28. He recites the verse, "He struck down Vṛtra... (VS 4.2.11b), and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
3.4.1.29. “Recite for the Viśve Devas,” he says, while spreading [the base] and cutting [the portion].
3.4.1.30. “O Viśve Devas, you who increase the cosmic order (ṛtāvṛdhas),” he recites.
3.4.1.31. “O Viśve Devas, hear this my invocation,” with these words he performs the sacrifice; when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
3.4.1.32. "Recite for Heaven and Earth," he says, as he places the cake on one potsherd, which has been spread with butter and sprinkled over.
3.4.1.33. "May Heaven and Earth [protect] this [offering] of ours," he recites.
3.4.1.34. "To the two first-born," he offers the sacrifice. At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation.
3.4.1.35. He consecrates the offering of the single-potherd cake that has been sacrificed with the mantra:

'After the sacrifices,' he consecrates the single-potherd cake that has been sacrificed: 'May we prosper after cattle, after horses, after all nourishments, after offspring, and after power; O gods, may you lead our sacrifice straightway.'"

3.4.2.2. If it should turn over, having set it upright and offered with the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā*, he should offer with the two subsequent verses: “May you be established through sacrifices, through wealth, through horses, through all prosperity, through offspring, and through sensory power; may Vaiśvānara, the undeceived, protect us from all misfortunes within with well-being, Svāhā! May your strengths, may your words, may your milks, may your heights, and may your joints come to the sacrifice joint by joint, Svāhā!”—thus.
3.4.2.3. Reciting, “For Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, after [the portion], svāhā!,” he spreads a base of clarified butter while taking the portions.
3.4.2.4. He takes a single portion from the northern half of each of all the oblations.
3.4.2.5. Having taken a portion from the cake baked on one potsherd from its receptacle, he pours clarified butter over it twice.
3.4.2.6. He does not anoint [the offering-spoons]. 3.4.2.7. He recites as the two *saṃyājyā* verses the two *gāyatrī* verses beginning with, “O Agni, awaken with a hymn” (4.1.11t).
3.4.2.8. He performs the offering with the verse, “He is the bearer of oblations” (4.1.11u).
3.4.2.9. He offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
3.4.2.10. Having stepped across and set [the ladle] down in its proper place, he cuts off the *prāśitra*.
3.4.2.11. Having touched water, he cuts off the *iḍā*.
3.4.2.12. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places [the portion] for the *āgnīdhra*.
3.4.2.13. They consume [the portions]; they sprinkle themselves; they carry [the portions] around. 3.4.2.14.
When the *prāśitra* has been consumed by the *brahman*, the *āgnīdhra* sits down at the rubbish heap (*utkara*) with a water-pot.
3.4.2.15. He gives a garment; he gives the first-born calf; to him for whom there is the *āgrayaṇa* [sacrifice], he gives *khārīs* [of grain]. 3.4.2.16.
He offers the oblation for the *hotṛ* priest continuously.
3.4.2.17. The ritual procedure is completed up to the *patnī-homa*.

3.4.2.18. Following the *patnī-homa*, he offers two oblations with the *sruva*-ladle, [reciting]: “Thou art the messenger of the year, the image... (RV 10.85.6). 3.4.2.19. The Soma-related rite is thus completed. 3.4.2.20. Having placed together portions of the other sacrificial offerings, he sits down to the south and eats the sacrificer’s portion three times, [reciting]: “The gods have led us from good to better” (RV 10.14.14) and “Through thee, in thy pleasant dwelling... (ibid. 15).
3.4.2.21. "The rite is accomplished; it comes to rest. Thus ends the fourth section (anuvāka).
3.5–6. Brahmanhood.

The Brahman priest is chosen; having placed the sacrificial cord over his left shoulder and sipped water, he takes the fire into himself with two verses: “I first take Agni into myself,” and “The Agni who is within our hearts, O fathers” (TS 5.7.9a).

3.5.1.2. He touches [the earth] with his hand, saying: “May I be able for the sake of action and for the gods; for the sake of power and for the sake of good deed. 3.5.1.3. Saying, “Bṛhaspati is the Brahman,” he enters between the altar (vedi) and the rubbish heap (utkara).

3.5.1.4. Saying, “May he protect the sacrifice, may he protect the lord of the sacrifice, may he protect me, may he protect the rule of the sacrifice,” he steps across the rear of the altar and says, “Daidhiṣavyā!”

3.5.1.5. He takes a blade of grass from where he is about to sit down, [saying]: “Rise up from here; sit in the seat of another, he who is more immature than we. 3.5.1.6. With the words, “Parāvasu is cast out,” he throws away the blade of grass.
3.5.1.7. Having made a lap with the words, “Here I sit in the seat of life,” he sits down.

3.5.1.8. Having sat down, he mutters: "O God Savitṛ, this [person] chooses you, Bṛhaspati, the divine Brahman. Declare that to the mind; the mind to the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī to the Triṣṭubh; the Triṣṭubh to the Jagatī; the Jagatī to the Anuṣṭubh; the Anuṣṭubh to the Paṅkti; the Paṅkti to the Vasus; the Vasus to the Rudras; the Rudras to the Ādityas; the Ādityas to the Viśve Devas; the Viśve Devas to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati to the Brahman. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Bṛhaspati!"
"I am Brahmā among the gods; may he attain that [state] who would either speak against me or seek to scrutinize me: *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar*, *om*, I am so-and-so, the man. 3.5.1.9.
While the *praṇītā* waters are being brought forward, he should restrain his speech until the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*).
3.5.1.10. When he says, "O Brahman, I shall bring forward the waters; O sacrificer, restrain your speech," [he should do so].

3.5.1.11. He pronounces this [formula]: “Lead forth the sacrifice; cause these deities to prosper. May the sacrificer be upon the back of the firmament, where the world of the seven seers who have performed good deeds is located; place this sacrifice and the sacrificer there—Oṃ, lead forth! 3.5.1.12. While the *stambayajus* is being carried away from the northern enclosure-line. 3.5.1.13.
When he says, “O Brahman, I shall perform the northern enclosure-line,” [the Brahman responds].

3.5.1.14. He impels it [the altar] with: “O Bṛhaspati, encompass the altar; may it be dear to the gods. May it be pleasant; strew the sacrificial grass within its lap. May the lap of Aditi be auspicious for us; encompass it. 3.5.1.15.

While the *sāmidhenī* verses are being recited, he restrains his speech until the concluding formula (*paridhāna*). 3.5.1.16. While each *puro’nuvākyā* verse is being recited, he restrains his speech until the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

3.5.1.17. Whenever he performs [an action] with either a *ṛc* or a *yajus*, he restrains his speech until the concluding verse (*paridhānīya*). 3.5.1.18. If he were to release his speech in the interval, he would cut the sacrifice asunder.

3.5.1.19. Now, if he should release it through negligence, he should recite a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "O Viṣṇu, you who are our closest, grant us protection, O Conqueror! Your streams, dripping with honey, flow forth; they milk out that which is inexhaustible. (TS 3.1.10k)
3.5.1.20. While the *prāśitra* portion is being cut off, he restrains his speech.
While the *prāśitra* is being cut off, he restrains his speech until the impulse (*prasava*).
3.5.2.2. When he offers him the *prāśitra* (the portion for consumption), he touches water and gazes at it, saying: "I gaze upon you with the eye of Sūrya.
3.5.2.3. He receives it, saying: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you.
3.5.2.4. "I set you down in the lap of the Earth," he says.
3.5.2.5. Regarding these two, some eat from them; others, disregarding that [rule], should eat from these two alone with the formula: "I eat thee with the mouth of Agni."

3.5.2.6. Having sprinkled [the vessel] with water and having passed over the teeth [with the formula], "With the belly of Brāhmaṇaspati, with the sacred word of Bṛhaspati," he washes these [remnants] toward that direction in front of the right knee. Having poured them out and rinsed [the vessel], he places the *prāśitra-haraṇa* and the portion for the Brahman priest into it, purifies it with water, and touches his vital organs [with the formula]: "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils; may strength be in my thighs; may speed be in my knees; may my limbs be unharmed; do not harm me. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 10.72).

3.5.2.7. When he says, "O Brahman, we shall set forth," and having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he gives the impulse with the words, "O Āgnīdh, cleanse the fire once, once! (ĀpŚS 21.8).
